assessments.assessment: The applications, listed materials, distinction between small-deformation stiffness and large-deformation/failure behavior, and dependence on material/specimen/loading experiments all survive in coherent English. No universal material law or safety promise is introduced.

Tension/compression testing is distinguished from the particular ductile uniaxial-tension schematic. Engineering stress uses original cross-sectional area; engineering strain uses original gauge length. True stress using the changing area is explicitly excluded. OA is the linear proportional region, and proportional limit remains conditional on the experiment and criterion, rather than a universal threshold.
The empty fig-88 placeholder is preserved, with English label Figure 88; no instructional task or answer was inserted.
The caption is translated as Figure 88 and retains its figure identity.

Nonlinearity beyond the proportional limit is not equated with appreciable permanent deformation. AB retains approximately recoverable deformation after unloading. The no-more-than 0.1% residual-strain convention and one-percent difference are correctly attributed to the textbook and explicitly denied universal exactness.

Plastic deformation is the permanent part remaining after unloading, distinct from recoverable elastic deformation. The conditional wording for the illustrated kind of material and the caveat against identical plastic stages in every material are retained.

C and CD describe appreciable plastic extension at approximately unchanged tensile force. Flow is identified as plastic yielding of a solid, not liquefaction. A pronounced horizontal plateau is restricted to some materials and experimental conditions, without requiring all tensile curves to have one.

Strain hardening raises the engineering-stress curve to maximum E; possible necking follows, and fracture is K after the maximum. Ultimate strength is the maximum engineering stress in this experiment. Lower force with shrinking local area does not require decreasing true stress at the neck. Neither strictly constant force throughout fracture nor the same sequence for brittle materials is asserted. Processing and test-condition dependence are retained.

Allowable stress remains below ultimate strength for this strength-margin definition. The translated formula n = sigma_ultimate / sigma_allowable has the correct numerator and denominator and retains equation (6-6). Working stress must not exceed allowable stress. The explicit exclusions for deformation, stability, fatigue, connections and other failure conditions prevent the ratio from becoming an unconditional structural-safety claim.

Material properties, static/dynamic loads, consequences and uncertainty remain factors in selecting n. The 1.7 to 10 interval is an attributed illustration, not a fixed universal range or design standard. Formula (6-6) determines allowable stress only after selecting an appropriate factor for the actual engineering conditions; the illustrative interval alone cannot establish real-structure safety.

languageAssessment: The full English lesson is grammatical and understandable in context. Technical terms (proportional limit, elastic limit, engineering stress/strain, plastic yielding, strain hardening, necking, ultimate strength, allowable stress and factor of safety) are used consistently. Ordinate and abscissa are explicitly explained. Paragraph and heading changes do not change meaning or omit any approved qualification.
